guard: the delivery daemon distinguishes 'the broker is gone' from 'this process did not get scheduled' — it stays up and serves under local starvation, and still exits when the broker is genuinely gone or its lease is genuinely held by another daemon (#1318)
why: THE DEFAULT COMMAND IS THE PURE SUITE, AND THAT IS A DELIBERATE CHOICE ABOUT WHAT CAN BE
GRADED. Every mutation edits a predicate in watchdog.ts, which the pure suite imports RELATIVELY,
so tsx loads the mutated source with no dist in the path and no build step between the edit and
the run. The live suite spawns a real daemon through bin/cotal.ts, which resolves the package to
its BUILD, so the two -live mutations build first and rebuild in afterRestore. They are the two
whose end-to-end consequence IS the incident, and they must be shown to reach a real process.
THE THREE SIGNALS, AND A MUTATION FOR EACH. The repair rests on evidence rather than elapsed
time, and the evidence has three independent sources: (a) the gap between consecutive firings of
the daemon own timer, (b) whether a probe RAN and refused within the time the server was actually
given, and (c) whether this daemon own connection to that broker is still open. M3 removes (a),
M2/M7/M9 attack the two halves of (b), M1 removes the requirement for any of them, and M4/M5/M6
are the controls on the guarantees the repair must not trade away.
M1 IS THE DEFECT IN ITS SHORTEST FORM: elapsed wall-clock alone decides the broker is gone. It is
the shipped predicate restored. The starvation cells redden and the broker-killed cells stay
green, which is the asymmetry the issue is about: the old code was not wrong about dead brokers,
it was wrong about busy hosts.
M2 AND M7 ARE THE TWO FORMS OF STARVATION A COMPLETED PROBE CAN TAKE, and they are separate
mutations because they are separate clauses catching separate conditions. M2 is the LOUD form the
triage captured: an answer at 2.5x its own budget, self-evidently not a statement about the
server, caught with no instrumentation at all. M7 is the QUIET form the measured incident was
actually made of: the probe completes looking prompt, while the process was off the runqueue for
nearly all of it and the server was given 40ms of its second. Cell E of the live suite is what
established that M2 clause alone could not see this, and M7-live grades it against a real daemon
on a ~10% duty cycle.
M9 IS THE CONTROL ON M7, and it is the one that keeps the repair from being a band-aid. Drop the
requirement that the probe actually ran out its budget and a starved host excuses EVERY refusal,
including the ~1ms ECONNREFUSED from a genuinely dead port: a daemon that outlives its broker
whenever the host is busy. K2 and K5 are the pair that pins it — same measured starvation,
opposite readings, decided solely by whether the answer beat the budget.
M8 IS THE CONTROL ON THE MEASUREMENT ITSELF. A sampler that charges the whole timer gap rather
than the excess over its own interval reports a healthy host as permanently starved, which slows
the exit when the broker really is gone. It survived the first time this fixture ran: cells L1-L5
drive stop() directly for determinism, so the timer callback never fired in any of them. L6 and
L7 pass real time specifically to let it fire.
M4 AND M5 AND M6 ARE THE CONTROLS ON THE GUARANTEES, and they matter more than the rest because
the failure mode this repair could introduce — a daemon that outlives a dead broker, or two
daemons serving one shard — is WORSE than the defect it removes. M4 deletes the backstop that
bounds the starvation credit; M5 makes a lease genuinely held by another daemon keep serving; M6
makes an UNANSWERABLE lease question exit, which is the wrong last sequence: 0 line from the
measured incident. Each reddens exactly the cell standing for a preserved guarantee and leaves
every starvation cell green, which is what proves the suite grades both directions.

mutations.name: M1 the defect restored: elapsed wall-clock time alone decides the broker is gone
mutations.find:
const unstarvedMs = e.msSinceLastReachable - e.starvedMs;
  if (unstarvedMs <= e.windowMs) return { exit: false, reason: "starved" };
mutations.expectRed: C1 does NOT exit: 20s elapsed with zero completed probes
mutations.cell: C1 does NOT exit: 20s elapsed with zero completed probes
mutations.note: The shipped predicate restored in the place it actually lived: past the window with the transport down, exit on elapsed time alone — no starvation credit, no requirement that any probe completed. Anchored on two contiguous CODE lines rather than on the nearest comment, so a docs commit cannot quietly disarm it.

mutations.name: M1-live the same defect, graded end to end against a real daemon and a real broker
mutations.find:
const unstarvedMs = e.msSinceLastReachable - e.starvedMs;
  if (unstarvedMs <= e.windowMs) return { exit: false, reason: "starved" };
mutations.expectRed: E5 the daemon did NOT exit on answers its own scheduling delay produced
mutations.cell: E5 the daemon did NOT exit on answers its own scheduling delay produced
mutations.note: The shipped predicate restored, graded against a real daemon on a ~10% CPU duty cycle with a live broker: it exits saying "0 completed probes refused within their deadline" — it gathered no evidence at all and ended anyway, which is the incident. It reds cell E rather than cell C because C keeps its standing socket and the transport signal carries the verdict there; M1 removes the starvation credit and the evidence requirement, not the transport clause. The broker-killed cells stay green in the same run, which is the asymmetry the issue is about.

mutations.name: M2 a probe answer that arrived long past its own deadline counts against the broker again
mutations.find: if (elapsedMs > ceiling) return { counts: "starved", lateBy: elapsedMs - budgetMs };
mutations.expectRed: J4 a false at 2554ms on a 1000ms budget is STARVED, not a negative
mutations.cell: J4 a false at 2554ms on a 1000ms budget is STARVED, not a negative
mutations.note: The loud form of the signal, and the one the #1318 triage captured directly: a false at 2554ms against a 1000ms budget, from a broker that answered immediately either side of it. It is an INDEPENDENT safety net rather than a duplicate of M7 rule (2): when the sampler measures nothing — a stall inside a native call, a host where timer resolution hides it — an answer at 2.5x its own budget is still self-evidently not a statement about the server. J4 is where that is graded. It is graded in the PURE suite only, deliberately: the live blackhole ends probes AT their budget rather than past it, so no live cell here reaches this clause, and rather than contrive a live scenario to reach it I state the boundary.  keeps the binding used so the mutant compiles; a mutation that cannot build grades the compiler, not the suite.

mutations.name: M3 measured local starvation is observed and then ignored
mutations.expectRed: B1 does NOT exit: the same 20s window with 19s of measured loop lag
mutations.cell: B1 does NOT exit: the same 20s window with 19s of measured loop lag
mutations.note: The band-aid shape: the daemon measures its own scheduler lag, reports it, and does not let it change the verdict. Indistinguishable from the fix by inspection of the log lines alone.

mutations.name: M4 CONTROL: the starvation credit becomes unbounded, so a daemon can outlive a dead broker
mutations.find: if (e.msSinceLastReachable > e.backstopMs) return { exit: true, reason: "broker-gone" };
mutations.expectRed: F1 exits past the backstop even with zero completed probes and full starvation credit
mutations.cell: F1 exits past the backstop even with zero completed probes and full starvation credit
mutations.note: Positive control for the failure mode this repair could otherwise introduce, which is WORSE than the defect: a daemon that never exits loops reconnect attempts forever and nothing recovers it. Every starvation cell stays green and only the backstop cell reddens, which proves the two are graded independently.

mutations.name: M5 CONTROL: a lease genuinely held by another daemon no longer ends this one
mutations.expectRed: G5 STILL exits on `taken` — the single-holder guarantee is preserved
mutations.cell: G5 STILL exits on `taken` — the single-holder guarantee is preserved
mutations.note: Positive control for the guarantee the repair must preserve. Two daemons serving one shard SPLIT a durable's delivery, which is a correctness failure rather than an availability one.

mutations.name: M6 CONTROL: an unanswerable lease question is treated as a negative answer again
mutations.expectRed: G3 REFUSES to exit on `unknown` — an unanswerable question is not a negative answer
mutations.cell: G3 REFUSES to exit on `unknown` — an unanswerable question is not a negative answer
mutations.note: The incident's second exit line, `lost the lease (wrong last sequence: 0)`, in decision form. The genuine-takeover cell stays green in the same run, so the refusing case and the accepting case are graded separately rather than by one assertion.

mutations.name: M7 the quiet form of starvation is invisible again: a probe is judged by the clock alone
mutations.expectRed: K4 a 1000ms false of which 960ms was off-CPU is STARVED, not a negative
mutations.cell: K4 a 1000ms false of which 960ms was off-CPU is STARVED, not a negative
mutations.note: The condition the measured incident was actually in: the timer fires, the probes complete, each one is a prompt-looking false that the server was never given time to answer. The loud-lateness rule (J) does not see it, which is why this clause exists and why it needs its own mutation.

mutations.name: M7-live the same, graded against a real daemon duty-cycled off the CPU
mutations.expectRed: E5 the daemon did NOT exit on answers its own scheduling delay produced
mutations.cell: E5 the daemon did NOT exit on answers its own scheduling delay produced
mutations.note: A real daemon on a ~10% duty cycle against a live broker. Without this clause it exits with "2 completed probes refused within their deadline" — the incident, reproduced end to end.

mutations.name: M8 the deschedule sampler charges ordinary timer jitter as starvation
mutations.expectRed: L6 an idle real-time span charges only the excess, not the whole gap
mutations.cell: L6 an idle real-time span charges only the excess, not the whole gap
mutations.note: CONTROL on the measurement itself. A sampler that counts the whole gap rather than the EXCESS over its own interval reports a healthy host as permanently starved, which would make the daemon slow to exit when the broker really is gone — the failure mode worse than the defect, arriving through the measurement rather than through the predicate. It SURVIVED the first run of this fixture: L1-L5 drive stop() directly for determinism, so the timer callback never fired in any of them and the clause was unreachable. L6 is the cell that actually grades it, by passing real time and letting the callback run.

mutations.name: M9 CONTROL: measured starvation excuses even a refusal that beat its budget
mutations.expectRed: K2 a dead port answers in ~1ms, and that is a negative however starved the host is
mutations.cell: K2 a dead port answers in ~1ms, and that is a negative however starved the host is
mutations.note: The band-aid this clause could so easily have been: drop the requirement that the probe actually ran out its budget, and a starved host excuses EVERY refusal, including the ~1ms ECONNREFUSED from a genuinely dead port. That is a daemon that outlives its broker whenever the host is busy. K2/K5 are the pair that pins it: same measured starvation, opposite readings, decided by whether the answer beat the budget.

mutations.name: M10 CONTROL: ordinary timer jitter excuses an honest budget-ended refusal again
mutations.expectRed: M1 a budget-ended refusal with ordinary timer jitter is a NEGATIVE, not starvation
mutations.cell: M1 a budget-ended refusal with ordinary timer jitter is a NEGATIVE, not starvation
mutations.note: A REVIEWER FINDING, and the subtlest failure in this PR. Requiring merely attributable < budget means ANY non-zero measurement disqualifies a budget-ended refusal, and ordinary Node timer jitter on a healthy host measures 10-30ms: 10 of 10 blackholed probes read STARVED on an unstarved box. The exit guarantee survives (the backstop still fires) but the EVIDENCE path becomes unreachable in production, so a genuinely dead broker is ended four times slower than the shipped window with the wrong reason in the log. The material-share line is what separates "the server got almost none of its second" from "the server got 984ms of it".

mutations.name: M11 CONTROL: every probe is judged against a budget the ws transport never had
mutations.expectRed: M6 the probe budget is the transport's own: ws gets 5s, tcp gets 1s
mutations.cell: M6 the probe budget is the transport's own: ws gets 5s, tcp gets 1s
mutations.note: A REVIEWER FINDING. isReachable gives a ws(s) broker 5s because it rides an HTTPS edge; judging its honest 2-5s refusals against a hardcoded 1000 files every one as this process starvation, so a dead ws broker can never accumulate a single completed negative. Same shape as M10: the guarantee holds, the evidence path does not.

mutations.name: M12 CONTROL: a departing daemon deletes its replacement lease on the way out
mutations.find:
if (revision === undefined) return;
    try { await (await this.deliveryRegistry()).delete(leaseKey(shardIndex), { previousSeq: revision }); }
mutations.expectRed: F7 the replacement STILL holds a live, ready lease after the loser finished exiting
mutations.cell: F7 the replacement STILL holds a live, ready lease after the loser finished exiting
mutations.note: A REVIEWER FINDING, and the merge blocker. Every takeover path ends in shutdown(1), and shutdown released the lease with an UNCONDITIONAL KV delete. By the time a daemon exits because another daemon took the shard, the row belongs to the replacement — so the polite release deleted the new holder lease and left the shard unserved. That is the #1318 outage again, reached through the lease path instead of the broker watch. Only a live cell can see it: leaseAction was always correct, and the damage happened downstream of the decision.
